content: The essay states the qualification the annotation offers as a refutation, in the paragraphs the annotation quotes: good authorities know about counterevidence, so the screening is exact only for a complete argument. That is the standard structure of an idealization — the title names the limiting case, the body gives the correction — and the essay's practical claim is the comparative one, that as the argument you have seen becomes more complete, the residual weight of the credential falls. Nothing in the d-separation objection touches that, and the essay's example of Jaynes and an erratum is a case where it was right.

quote: But this slight strength of authority is only ceteris paribus, and can easily be overwhelmed by stronger arguments.
content: "Slight" is the essay's estimate for the specific case it is discussing, a reader who has followed a technical argument to its end, and the essay says the weight "can easily be overwhelmed by stronger arguments," which is a conditional and not a constant. The demand for a likelihood ratio is fair and it is the essay's own framework; the number varies by field, by the completeness of the argument, and by whether the expert has seen counterevidence the reader has not, all of which the essay names. A ratio that "can be very large" in mature fields is compatible with its being small once you can check the algebra, which is the case under discussion.
